name: Oulu
title: Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging Oulu | Tankers, Feeders, Bulk
description: Ship thickness measurement in Oulu at Oritkari and Vihreäsaari: UTM of product tanker, container feeder and bulk carrier hull, tanks and ice belt structure.
h1: Thickness Measurement for Ships at the Port of Oulu
intro: Oulu is the largest city in northern Finland, and its port near the head of the Bay of Bothnia supplies the region with fuel and takes out its forest products. Product tankers berth at Vihreäsaari, container feeders and general cargo ships at Oritkari, and ice-class ships keep calling through a long frozen season. That gives gauging work on tank structure, decks and ice belts. For every job, Atlantis flies technicians from India to the ship and plans the visit around her cargo days.

highlights.p: Vihreäsaari is where tankers bring oil products for Oulu and the wide country to the north and east. These ships trade here through the winter on tight supply schedules, so deck, piping and ballast-tank gauging is fitted into discharge rather than given its own port stay.

highlights.h: Forest products and feeders at Oritkari
highlights.p: Oritkari, the main general cargo harbour, handles containers and forest products. Feeder ships on fixed rotations to larger hub ports call regularly, which lets a gauging scope be spread over several visits and finished in good time before a docking.

highlights.h: One of the Baltic's longest ice seasons
highlights.p: Near the head of the Bay of Bothnia, sea ice usually arrives early and leaves late. Ships calling at Oulu in winter need high ice classes and icebreaker escort, and their ice belts show it, with heavy coating loss and local wastage to measure each spring.

port.h: Port of Oulu: harbours, traffic and the ice year
p: The Port of Oulu sits where the Oulujoki river meets the Bay of Bothnia, and its harbours lie on islands and reclaimed land around the city's waterfront. Oritkari is the main cargo harbour, built for containers, general cargo and forest products, with sheds and open storage behind the quay. Vihreäsaari is the oil and bulk harbour, where tankers discharge fuels and dry bulk is handled. A mill harbour at Nuottasaari serves the forest industry beside it. The approach comes in from the open Bay of Bothnia through a buoyed fairway across shallow coastal water, and as elsewhere on this coast the Baltic has almost no tide, so depths at the berths change with wind-driven water level rather than with the moon.

Oulu's traffic is regional supply and export. Product tankers bring petrol, diesel and heating oil for the city and for the sparsely populated north, and dry bulk for industry, energy and agriculture comes in across the quays. Outbound, the region's pulp, board and sawn timber move in containers and as general cargo, while container feeders link Oulu to larger hub ports elsewhere in Europe. The ships are small to medium in size, with a high share of Finnish-Swedish ice classes among the regular callers, and some combine Oulu with other Bothnian ports on the same voyage. Port stays are usually measured in a day or two rather than in hours, which gives a gauging plan something to work with.

Ice defines the Oulu year. The sea in the northern Bay of Bothnia freezes every winter, and the ice season here is among the longest anywhere in the Baltic, often running from late autumn well into spring. Finnish and Swedish icebreakers work this area together, escorting ships through the fairways and keeping traffic moving to ports on both sides of the bay, and the Finnish winter traffic restrictions for Oulu are usually among the first to tighten and the last to lift. For a tanker on the winter supply run, months of escorted passage through compressed ice wear the coating off the bow and ice belt, and every spring brings owners wanting to know what the winter cost them in steel. The short, light summer is when dockings and planned survey work happen.

facilities.h: Where ships are gauged in Oulu
p: Tanker work at Vihreäsaari follows the oil terminal's rules and the ship's permit system. During discharge the team can measure deck plating, the outside of cargo, ballast and fuel lines, and ballast tanks that the crew has certified safe, while cargo tank internals wait for a gas-free period or the yard. At Oritkari, container feeders and general cargo ships are measured within their working day; on a feeder the scope is cut into pieces that each fit one call, with the ballast tanks and the ice belt from inside usually done first, and decks and coamings when the cargo plan allows.

Oulu is not a docking port for large merchant ships in our planning, so renewal surveys for the ships that trade here are normally carried out at repair yards in southern Finland, elsewhere in the Baltic or further afield. Pre-docking gauging at an Oulu call gives that yard the steel quantities in advance. In winter there is little room for work at anchor, because ships move straight from icebreaker escort to the berth, so all winter gauging at Oulu is planned alongside.

Vihreäsaari bulk berths — dry-bulk ships; hold and tank-top measurements as each hold is cleared
Oritkari harbour — container feeders, general cargo and forest-product ships; staged gauging of tanks, decks and coamings within each call

context.h: Rules and winter navigation behind Oulu gauging
p: Port state control at Oulu is Traficom's responsibility under the Paris MoU, with inspections targeted by ship type, age and record. Tankers count among the higher-risk types, and a product tanker that trades into Oulu every winter builds up the kind of history inspectors look at: corrosion in ballast tanks, deck pipework weakened by cold and condensation, and ice-belt wear. Oil companies and terminal operators vet the tankers they use, and a vetting inspection that finds heavy wastage on deck lines or in ballast tanks can lose a ship her place on the supply run, so tanker owners here often ask for gauging ahead of a vetting.

Winter navigation is the other framework. Each season the Finnish authorities publish traffic restrictions per port, setting the lowest ice class and the minimum ship size that can count on icebreaker assistance, and at Oulu the higher ice classes are needed for the longest part of the year. Under the Finnish-Swedish Ice Class Rules the ice class rests partly on ice-belt plating thickness, which includes an allowance for abrasion and corrosion that successive winters steadily use up. Ships trading into Oulu from outside the EU also carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, a document buyers and charterers now ask to see.

jobs.h: Common thickness measurement jobs at Oulu
jobs.p: The work in Oulu follows its two main trades and the ice. Tankers on the fuel supply run need their deck lines and ballast tanks measured regularly, often between vettings. Feeders and general cargo ships at Oritkari bring planned survey preparation, cut into pieces that fit their calls. Every spring adds a run of post-winter checks, as owners measure the ice belt and bow after months in compressed ice, and the short summer is when most pre-docking work is fitted in before the ships go to their yards. Pre-purchase gauging turns up when ice-class tonnage changes hands, because buyers want proof that the ice belt still meets the class.
list: Deck pipeline and ballast-tank gauging on a product tanker discharging at Vihreäsaari, ahead of an oil-company vetting
Post-winter ice-belt and bow gauging on an ice-class feeder at Oritkari, with frame and bracket crack checks where ice damage is reported
Renewal-survey preparation on a general cargo ship spread across two Oulu calls, so the steel list reaches the yard before the docking
Hatch cover and coaming gauging on a forest-product carrier loading at Oulu, after cargo receivers complained of water damage
Pre-purchase gauging on an ice-class tanker or feeder, with ice-belt figures and IHM status set out for the buyer

logistics: Oulu Airport, south-west of the city, is one of Finland's busiest airports, with frequent connections from Helsinki, so the team travels from India via Helsinki and drives on to Oritkari or Vihreäsaari. Finland is a Schengen country, and our technicians need Schengen visas, which we apply for as soon as the job date is firm. The ship's agent arranges ISPS passes for the harbours, and the oil terminal at Vihreäsaari runs its own safety induction. Winter itineraries carry a buffer for weather and icebreaker delays.

faqs.q: Can a product tanker be gauged during discharge at Vihreäsaari?
faqs.a: Part of the scope, yes. Deck plating, the external surface of cargo, ballast and fuel piping and ballast tanks certified safe by the crew can be measured during discharge, under the ship's and the terminal's permits. Cargo tank internals need gas-free certification, so for a renewal or CAP scope we plan them for a gas-free period or the docking. Deck work is planned so it never interferes with hose connections or manifold operations.

faqs.q: When is the best time of year for gauging at Oulu?
faqs.a: It depends on the purpose. Spring and early summer suit a post-winter check of the ice belt, because the damage is fresh and the readings can go straight into the summer docking plan. Autumn suits a pre-winter check, ahead of the traffic restrictions. Survey preparation inside tanks and holds can be done in any month; only shell work from outside is restricted when ice lies against the hull.

faqs.q: Do you work at anchor off Oulu?
faqs.a: Rarely. In the open season most ships go straight to the berth, and in winter they arrive under icebreaker escort and berth directly, so there is little time or safe access at anchor. We plan Oulu jobs alongside at Oritkari, Vihreäsaari or the mill harbour, where the team can work under the ship's permits and the terminal's safety rules.

faqs.q: Can you check ice damage after an incident in the Bay of Bothnia?
faqs.a: Yes. After a reported ice contact we measure the affected shell and frames from inside where they can be reached, look for thinning around dents, and use magnetic particle testing on frames, brackets and welds to find cracks. The findings go to the superintendent and to the class surveyor, who decides whether the ship can continue trading or needs repair before her next voyage.
